requirement.label: Upper-Division Requirements
requirement.description: 36 UD units overall are required. 20 units must be from Areas A (department courses focusing on East Asia, China, Japan, and Korea), and the remaining 16 units may be from either Areas A or B (or any other course offered on campus with strong East Asia-related content - department approval required). Please check the General Catalog and, if necessary, consult with the Undergraduate Advisor for the most recent offerings.

narrative:
MAJOR REGULATIONSPREREQUISITES Check the General Catalog for the prerequisites to all listed courses.
P/NP GRADING OPTION Not allowed for any major course (Prep or UD major), including courses applied to the major from other departments.
SUBSTITUTIONS In the major requirements permissible only by petition to the department chair and dean.
G.P.A REQUIREMENTS At least 2.0 overall UC average in all upper-division major courses and all courses (Prep and UD) for the major.
DOUBLE MAJORS With the approval of each department chairperson, up to a total of 8 units may be applied simultaneously to both UD majors.

nodes.title: Survey: History of Art in China
nodes.description: Chronological and thematic overview of the major traditions of Chinese art, Neolithic to modern, including ceramics and bronzes, Buddhist visual culture, paintings, calligraphy, garden design and imperial architecture, with an emphasis on historical context, regional diversity, and intercultural encounters.

nodes.title: Chinese Painting I
nodes.description: Chinese painting and theory, from beginnings through the fourteenth century. Introduction to major developments and masters in their cultural context with a focus on meaning and agency.

nodes.title: Chinese Painting I
nodes.description: Chinese painting and theory, from beginnings through the fourteenth century. Introduction to major developments and masters in their cultural context with a focus on meaning and agency.

nodes.title: Art and Modern China
nodes.description: An exploration of trends and issues in nineteenth and twentieth-century Chinese art, as China awakens and responds to the challenges of modernity and the West. Topics include the continuity of tradition, the exile identity, and trends after Tienanmen (1989).

nodes.title: The Art of the Chinese Landscape
nodes.description: Chinese approaches to landscape as subject matter in art, with a focus on painting and garden architecture. The course begins with the immortality cult in the Han Dynasty (206 B.C.-A.D.221) and ends with contemporary artists of the twentieth century.

nodes.title: Chinese Calligraphy: History and Aesthetics
nodes.description: Examines the different scripts in historical context, surveys significant movements and artists, and considers the ideas, theories and aesthetic principles that have enriched the art of writing to elite status in China.

nodes.title: Twentieth-Century Architecture
nodes.description: The history of architecture from 1900 to the present. Examination of modern and post-modern architecture and city planning in its social, political, and artistic context. The scope is global.

nodes.title: Major Works of Asian Literatures
nodes.description: An introduction to the diverse literary traditions of Asia through an examination of selected works. Regional focus on East, South, and SoutheastAsia varies.

nodes.title: Young Humans: Introduction to Childhood Studies
nodes.description: An introduction to interdisciplinary approaches to understanding and analyzing childhood and youth, including history of childhood, and childrens literature research, this course considers the role of childhood in human life, its construction across different periods and regions, different disciplinary perspectives on childhood, and contemporary approaches to deepening the understanding of children and their own views. By examining key critical texts, it considers childhood through multiple disciplinary perspectives, as well as childrens own co-creation of the performance of childhood and childrens voice, agency, activism, and rights.

nodes.title: Critical Childhood Studies
nodes.description: This seminar/capstone course on critical childhood studies will examine the burgeoning field of childhood studies across time periods and regions, employing varied disciplinary approaches to the study of childhood, including literary studies, history, art history, sociology, and other disciplines. Assignments will include weekly responses, leading a discussion of a scholarly work, a final paper on a subject related to student interest, and a presentation of the final paper topic.

nodes.title: Elementary Modern Chinese
nodes.description: The beginning course in Chinese. The student acquires a basic knowledge of the grammar, a limited general vocabulary, correct pronunciation, and an ability to read and understand simple texts. Weekly laboratory assignments support and enhance classroom learning.

nodes.title: First Year Chinese Heritage
nodes.description: Intended for Chinese heritage speakers who wish to learn to read and write Chinese. Content is similar to Chinese 1 with less emphasis on developing oral skills.

nodes.title: Elementary Modern Chinese
nodes.description: Continuation of Chinese 1.

nodes.title: First Year Chinese Heritage
nodes.description: Continuation of Chinese 1NH.

nodes.description: Continuation of Chinese 2NH.

nodes.description: Continuation of Chinese 5.

nodes.title: Contemporary Chinese Religions
nodes.description: Examines Chinese popular religion, Daoism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Christianity, and Islam as shaped and transformed by revolution and nationalism, and the recent rapid commercialization, urbanization, and globalization of China. Religiosity and changing notions of self, family, gender, community, and citizenship.

nodes.title: Popular Culture in Modern Chinese Societies
nodes.description: Provides an overview of Chinese popular culture from PRC, Taiwan, and Hong Kong, covering various media and genres such as popular literature, film, online culture, music, video games, and cartoons.

nodes.title: Nature and Ethics in Chinese Philosophy
nodes.description: A look at how major thinkers in classical Chinese thought grappled with questions related to the individual's place in society and their relationship to their environment. Highlighting their relevance, classical views will be applied to contemporary ethical, social, and environmental debates.

nodes.title: Masterpieces in Chinese Literature
nodes.description: Examines a selection of works from Chinese literature, with the goal of understanding the major genres and their development over time. The cultural roles of literature, as well as criteria for critical evaluation, are also addressed.

nodes.title: Modern Chinese Literature
nodes.description: This course, taught in English, surveys an archive of seminal short fiction, novellas, novels, and poems that tell the story of China and the Chinese from the end of the Qing dynasty to the present. What has been the place of literature in China in the modern era? What vision of modern China do we find in its literature? How, moreover, does literature subvert the national narrative? Through literature as a window on the history of modern China, students gain a better understanding of Chinese history and culture with regard to its social reform, revolution, war, cultural revolution, cultural revival, and economic growth.

nodes.title: Introduction to Classical Chinese
nodes.description: The grammar and vocabulary of classical Chinese. Readings concentrate on philosophical and historical works from the pre-Han period, with some selections from later prose and poetry. Students with some familiarity with Chinese characters (through another Asian language) but not modern Chinese will be accommodated.

nodes.title: Introduction to Classical Chinese
nodes.description: The grammar and vocabulary of classical Chinese. Readings concentrate on philosophical and historical works from the Pre-Han period, with some selections from later prose and poetry. Students with some familiarity with Chinese characters (through another Asian language) but not modern Chinese will be accommodated.

nodes.title: Reading and Writing in Chinese
nodes.description: Designed to enhance reading and writing skills in Chinese for students who have finished second year Chinese.

nodes.title: Third-Year Chinese I
nodes.description: Advanced practice in grammar and composition.

nodes.title: Third-Year Chinese II
nodes.description: Advanced practice in grammar and composition.

nodes.title: Third-Year Chinese III
nodes.description: Advanced practice in grammar and composition.

nodes.title: Readings in Taiwan Literature
nodes.description: Offers a close reading of postwar Taiwan and exile literature from the 1940s to the present, and provides a basic introduction to literary criticism and analysis. Taught in English, the assigned texts are in traditional Chinese and English translations will be provided.

nodes.title: Advanced Chinese in Practice I
nodes.description: Course series for students who have advanced levels in Chinese. Extensive reading and discussion of various styles and practices of the Chinese language in addition to topics on modern and contemporary China. Teaching materials from literary works, newspapers, internet, and films.

nodes.title: Advanced Chinese in Practice II
nodes.description: Course series for students who have advanced levels in Chinese. Extensive reading and discussion of various styles and practices of the Chinese language in addition to topics on modern and contemporary China. Teaching materials from literary works, newspapers, internet, and films.

nodes.title: Advanced Chinese in Practice III
nodes.description: Course series for students who have advanced levels in Chinese. Extensive reading and discussion of various styles and practices of the Chinese language in addition to topics on modern and contemporary China. Teaching materials from newspaper, internet, and films.

nodes.title: Chinese Painting I
nodes.description: Chinese painting and theory, from beginnings through the fourteenth century. Introduction to major developments and masters in their cultural context with a focus on meaning and agency.

nodes.title: Art and Modern China
nodes.description: An exploration of trends and issues in nineteenth and twentieth-century Chinese art, as China awakens and responds to the challenges of modernity and the West. Topics include the continuity of tradition, the exile of identity, and the trends after Tiananmen (1989)

nodes.title: Chinese Calligraphy- History and Aesthetics
nodes.description: Examines the different scripts in historical context, surveys significant movements and artists, and considers the ideas, theories and aesthetic principles that have enriched the art of writing to elite status in China.

nodes.title: Special Topics in Taiwan Studies - Humanities
nodes.description: Special topics in Taiwan studies with respect to literature, history, and culture from the period of Japanese rule (1895-1945) to the present, including modernity, national identity, intellectual movements, and popular culture. Topics and reads will vary with instructors.

nodes.title: China in Translation: Theory, Art, History
nodes.description: Uses case studies of translations into and out of China--long regarded as a civilization distinct from the West--to explore themes in translation studies. Topics include ideograms, orientalism, modernization, world literature, annotation, musicality, poetic license, and adaptation.

nodes.title: Tang Literary History
nodes.description: Examines the history of literature during the celebrated Tang dynasty (618907). Focus on changes in literary norms, practices, and theory as they intersected with societal, political, intellectual, and religious developments. Also considers problems of historiography. Emphasis varies by quarter.

nodes.title: Urban Legends: Traditional Chinese Stories and Their Afterlives
nodes.description: Masterworks of fiction from the Ming and Qing periods as products of urban culture in late imperial and contemporary China. Stories by Feng Menglong, Li Yu, tales by Pu Songling, and excerpts from classic novels.

nodes.title: Women Writers of Late Imperial China
nodes.description: A study of Chinese women writers in the late imperial period (roughly 1500-1900), a newly rediscovered part of China's literary history. Examination of their personal lives and writings in relation to the Chinese literary tradition, women's history and feminist criticism.

nodes.title: Poetic Culture in late Imperial China and Beyond
nodes.description: An examination of the role poetry played in both social and individual lives in late imperial China, with particular attention to self-expression and literary community. Relevant practices in later times and in Japan and Korea are also covered.

nodes.title: Storytelling and Chinese Culture
nodes.prereq_text: Reading knowledge and skills in advanced modern Chinese
nodes.description: Taught in Chinese, this course is designed to elucidate Chinese history and culture from the perspective of storytelling. Readings are original narrative texts from the Tang, Song, and Ming-Qing eras.

nodes.title: History of Sexuality in China
nodes.description: Examines the role of gender and sexual relations in the development of politics, society, culture, and personal life in China and the Sinophone world.

nodes.title: Queer China, Crip China
nodes.description: In this course we study the representation of non-normative bodyminds and desires (e.g. disability and homosexuality) in modern Chinese literature and film. We discuss the meanings embedded in Chinese discourses of gender, sexuality, and disability; investigate how these discourses have been appropriated in the construction of a modern Chinese national identity; and connect our specific inquiry into Queer China and Crip China to our general attempt to answer the broader question of how the modern nation-state China has been imagined into being over the past century. Our approach is interdisciplinary, comparative, and transnational.

nodes.title: Fiction and Film in Contemporary China
nodes.description: Presents a critical historical overview of Chinese literature and film from 1949 to the present. In addition to writers and filmmakers from mainland China such as Mo Yan and Zhang Yimou, course considers literary and cinematic development from Hong Kong, Taiwan, and the Chinese diaspora.

nodes.title: Chinese Cinema: Nationalism and Globalism
nodes.prereq_text: upper division standing or instructor approval
nodes.description: A critical overview of some of the major cinematic trends in Chinese-language film over the past several decades. Works from the PRC, Taiwan and Hong Kong, as well as Chinese cinema will be considered in a global context.

nodes.title: Religious Practice and the State in China
nodes.description: Historical and anthropological approaches to the interaction between religious practice and state forces, with emphasis on popular religion and the decline and revival of religion in Chinese modernity.

nodes.title: Qing Empire
nodes.prereq_text: A prior course in History or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: The Qing period saw the doubling of China's territory, the enormous population growth, and the many encounters with the West. We will examine the politics, cultures, social norms, and different peoples, with a focus on the problem of modernization.

nodes.title: Modern China (since 1911)
nodes.prereq_text: Any lower-division course in History or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: The fall of the dynastic system, the revolution against traditional values, the rise of the Nationalist Party, the challenge from the Communists, the founding of the People's Republic, and the Post-Mao reform, with a focus on the theme of revolution.

nodes.title: Undergrad Research Seminar on Modern China
nodes.prereq_text: History 185A or 185B or Chin 185A or Chin 185B or HIST 185CQ or CHIN 185CQ and upper division standing.
nodes.description: Research seminar in the history of modern China. Students will conduct historical research in a seminar context, using both primary and secondary source materials, to produce an original and substantial research paper.

nodes.title: History of Modern Chinese Thought
nodes.prereq_text: HIST 2A-B-C or HIST 80 or HIST/CHIN 184A-B or HIST/CHIN 185A-B or EACS 4A-B
nodes.description: Leads students to understand some of the most important ideas, theories, and concepts in Modern China.

nodes.title: Readings in Chinese
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Chinese.

items.text: completion of 2 upper-division courses in Chinese

nodes.description: Readings in Chinese.

nodes.title: Independent Studies in Chinese
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Chinese major; Minimum major GPA of 3.5 or higher

items.text: completion of 2 upper-division courses in Chinese major

nodes.description: Independent studies in Chinese. Individual investigations in literary fields.

nodes.title: Introduction to Asian Religious Traditions
nodes.description: An introduction to the basic texts, institutions, and practices of the religious traditions of South Asia and East Asia.

nodes.title: East Asian Traditions: Pre-modern
nodes.description: An introduction to the social structures, institutions, systems of thought and belief, and the arts and entertainments of China, Japan, Korea and their neighbors during the pre-modern period.

nodes.title: East Asian Traditions: Modern
nodes.description: An introduction to the study of China, Japan, Korea, and their neighbors in modern times, including the process of modernization, intellectual and political movements, national identity, literature and the arts, and popular culture.

nodes.title: Introduction to Buddhism
nodes.description: The historical and cross-cultural exploration of Buddhism through the examination of basic texts, institutions, and practices of diverse Buddhist traditions.

nodes.title: Zen Buddhism
nodes.description: An introduction to the history and texts of the major lineages of Ch`an Buddhism in China and Zen Buddhism in Japan.

nodes.title: Gender and Sexuality in Modern Asia
nodes.description: Examines how modern social institutions have constructed and transformed gender and sexuality in China, Japan, Korea, India, and other Asian societies. Topics: marriage and kinship, capitalism, nationalism, modern state, third genders, commercialization of sex, public sphere and mass media.

nodes.title: Young Humans: Introduction to Childhood Studies
nodes.description: An introduction to interdisciplinary approaches to understanding and analyzing childhood and youth, including history of childhood, and childrens literature research, this course considers the role of childhood in human life, its construction across different periods and regions, different disciplinary perspectives on childhood, and contemporary approaches to deepening the understanding of children and their own views. By examining key critical texts, it considers childhood through multiple disciplinary perspectives, as well as childrens own co-creation of the performance of childhood and childrens voice, agency, activism, and rights.

nodes.title: Introduction to Daoism
nodes.description: A study of the classical sources of Daoism, followed by a consideration of the varieties of religious practice which developed from those sources.

nodes.title: Sex, Science, and Society: A Global History
nodes.description: Survey of the relationship between sex, science, and society in the history of the modern world. Emphasis on the development of scientific ideas about the human body against broader social, cultural, and political trends and from a global viewpoint.

nodes.title: Chinese Civilization
nodes.description: A survey of the history of Chinese civilization from 2,000 BCE to the present, focusing on the origins and later development of political, social, economic, philosophical, religious, and cultural traditions.

nodes.title: Anthropology of China
nodes.description: This course adopts an anthropological approach to contemporary China through ethnographic research. Topics include: Maoist society, rural life, migrant workers, gender and sexuality, media culture, youth culture, the urban work unit, from Maoist class-status system to capitalist class structure.

nodes.title: Anthropology of Japan
nodes.description: This course examines Japan as depicted in contemporary ethnography. We consider how Japan has been imagined as a distinct culture by exploring gender, religion, family structures, the education system, the environment, management of difference, globalization and domestication, immigration, and modernization.

nodes.title: Anthropology of Contemporary Korea
nodes.description: This course is an introduction to contemporary Korea covering the major societal transformations since the Korean War. Topics include nationalism, the creation of national symbols and racial identity, family, marriage, consumption, television dramas, globalization, tourism, and new Korean Wave.

nodes.title: Christianity, Judaism, and Islam in China
nodes.description: Examines Christian, Jewish, and Muslim communities in the Middle Kingdom from 500 to the present day, debunking the myth of a closed and insular China.

nodes.title: Religious Environmentalism in the Anthropocene: Asia & U.S.
nodes.description: What can ancient religious traditions do for environmental protection? This class examines doctrinal examples, both potential and actual, of religious environmentalism in China, India, Japan, and the U.S.: with Buddhism, Daoism, Hinduism, Shinto, and Protestantism.

nodes.title: Global East Asia
nodes.description: Offers an overview of theories about migration and globalization, coupled with the case studies from contemporary East Asia. Students investigate diverse transnational issues in and from this region, including ethnicity, nationalism, kinship, homeland, and colonialism.

nodes.title: Social Movements in East Asia
nodes.description: This course engages with cultural histories of social movements and political protests in modern and contemporary East Asia. All reading, viewing, and listening material will be available in English translation.

nodes.title: Transpacific Literature
nodes.description: Looks at the Pacific as the primary location for literary and historical imagination since the Age of Exploration. Studies the crisscross, transpacific field of inscriptions ranging from Captain Cook to Herman Melville, Mark Twain, Jack London, and Maxine Hong Kingston.

nodes.title: Literary Adaptation in East Asia
nodes.description: Explores literary adaptation and intertextuality in East Asia through primary texts and readings from critical theory. Among the texts considered are traditional poetry, The Tale of Genji, Chinese "strange tales" and representations of history and literature in film.

nodes.title: Introduction to Daoism
nodes.description: A study of the classical sources of Daoism, followed by a consideration of the varieties of religious practice which developed from those sources.

nodes.title: Medical Humanities in East Asia
nodes.description: Major concepts and issues at the intersection of healthcare and the humanities in modern East Asia. Topics may include narrative medicine, medicalization, body/embodiment, medical pluralism, mental health, social justice, and interdisciplinary approaches to systems of treatment and healing.

nodes.title: Sinophone Studies
nodes.description: The study of Sinitic-language communities and cultures around the world, marked by heterogeneity, placed-based practices, and differentiated relations to geopolitical units. Emphases will be on the questions of power, colonialism, hierarchy, resistance, plurality, and interdisciplinarity.

nodes.title: East Asian Buddhist Poetry
nodes.description: Introduces Buddhist poetry of China, Japan, and Korea. Emphasizes the diversity of literary encounters with the teachings and practices of Buddhism. Topics include Hanshan, Basho, Zen koans, Gary Snyder, and monastery cats.

nodes.title: The Modern Girl Around the World
nodes.description: Examines the Modern Girl as a historical phenomenon of the early twentieth century from the combined perspective of global history and gender history.

nodes.title: Buddhist Political Thought and Institutions
nodes.description: Buddhist political theories and practices in various Asian countries from antiquity to the present, with special emphasis on ideas of kinship and republicanism, state-formation process, cultural identity, and the interactions with other religions.

nodes.title: Visual Culture of Buddhism
nodes.description: This course explores the rich world of Buddhist visual culture, ranging from meditation to addressing the use of painted images in public performances. It focuses on sacred images, their rituals, and theories of representation behind their creation and use.

nodes.title: Critical Childhood Studies
nodes.description: This seminar/capstone course on critical childhood studies will examine the burgeoning field of childhood studies across time periods and regions, employing varied disciplinary approaches to the study of childhood, including literary studies, history, art history, sociology, and other disciplines. Assignments will include weekly responses, leading a discussion of a scholarly work, a final paper on a subject related to student interest, and a presentation of the final paper topic.

nodes.title: Internship
nodes.description: This internship allows students to collaborate with philanthropic, non-profit, and for-profit organizations that are based locally, nationally or globally. Working on-site or remotely, students learn practical implications of a degree in EALCS and in the Humanities more generally, and they have the opportunity to utilize their knowledge of technology and of foreign languages and cultures. While contributing to the organization and its initiatives, students gain valuable experience that can lead to career choices after graduation. Up to 4 units of internship can count towards an EALCS major or minor. Please see the EALCS website for information on arranging internships and for expectations regarding receiving internship credit.

nodes.title: Independent Study in Asian Studies
nodes.prereq_text: Upper division standing; completion of 2 upper division EACS courses; at least one of those two courses taken with the instructor for EACS 199; GPA for those two courses 3.5 or higher.

items.text: at least one of those two courses taken with the instructor for EACS 199

nodes.description: Independent Study under the supervision of a faculty member.

nodes.title: Transpacific Literature
nodes.description: Looks at the Pacific as the primary location for literary and historical imagination since the Age of Exploration. Studies the crisscross, transpacific field of inscriptions ranging from Captain Cook to Herman Melville, Mark Twain, Jack London, and Maxine Hong Kingston.

nodes.title: Introduction to Cinema
nodes.description: An introduction to the study of film as an aesthetic and social phenomenon, and to various methods of critical analysis.

nodes.title: Topics in National and Transnational Media: Japanese Anime
nodes.prereq_text: Film and Media Studies 46 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: A survey of Japanese animated films and TV shows from a theoretical perspective. Our focus is less on anim as a popular genre than on its potential to reconceptualize our experience of moving images in general. No prior knowledge of Japanese is required.

nodes.title: Global History, Culture and Ideology
nodes.description: A survey of the historical processes that have brought different areas of the world into closer contact. Topics include ideologies of nationalism, democracy, and liberalism; international trade and migrations; technological changes; colonialism; the globalization of culture; and the reactions to them.

nodes.title: Global Socioeconomic and Political Processes
nodes.description: Examination of contemporary social, economic, political, and environmental change in a global context; the emergence of a global economy and new systems of world order; and the debate over globalization and whether or not it is desireable.

nodes.title: Global Culture and Ethics
nodes.description: Explores connections over the last century between global cultural developments and the quest for normative values on a global level. Topics include the communications revolution, cultural ideologies, international migrations and diasporas, the human rights movement, and new cosmopolitanisms.

nodes.title: Global Ideologies and World Order
nodes.description: Deals with conceptions of the world as a unitary political system and how these views come into confrontation with one another. Topics include the nation-state system, political ideologies, international organizations, global conflict, and the emergent civil society.

nodes.title: World History
nodes.description: Survey of the peoples, cultures, and social, economic, and political systems that have characterized the world's major civilizations in Europe, Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Oceania from prehistory to 1000 CE.

nodes.title: World History
nodes.description: Survey of the peoples, cultures, and social, economic, and political systems that have characterized the world's major civilizations in Europe, Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Oceania from 1000 to 1700 CE.

nodes.title: World History
nodes.description: Survey of the peoples, cultures, and social, economic, and political systems that have characterized the world's major civilizations in Europe, Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Oceania from 1700 to present.

nodes.title: Historical Investigations: Methods and Skills
nodes.description: Through studying a particular topic in history, students gain insight into historical methods and skills. Course designed for freshmen and sophomore history majors or prospective majors. Others may enroll by permission of instructor. Topics vary by quarter and instructor.

nodes.title: Chinese Civilization
nodes.description: A survey of the history of Chinese civilization from 2,000 BCE to the present, focusing on the origins and later development of political, social, economic, philosophical, religious, and cultural traditions.

nodes.title: Japanese History Through Art and Literature
nodes.description: A basic introduction to the history of Japanese culture from its origins to the present day, with particular emphasis on the evidence of architecture and painting (presented through audiovisual modules). Selectedexamples of fiction and poetry will also be used.

nodes.title: Survey of South Asian History
nodes.description: An introduction to the history of the South Asian subcontinent, with emphasis on the period from 1500 CE to the present.

nodes.title: History of China
nodes.prereq_text: History 2A or 2B or 2C or 80 or EACS 80 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Ancient China to 589ce.

nodes.title: History of China
nodes.prereq_text: History 2A or 2B or 2C or 80 or EACS 80 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Sixth to seventeenth centuries.

nodes.title: History of Traditional Chinese Thought
nodes.description: A study of traditional Chinese thought from the classical period to the beginning of the last imperial dynasty (500 BCE -1700 CE).

nodes.title: Qing Empire
nodes.prereq_text: A prior course in History or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: The Qing period saw the doubling of China's territory, the enormous population growth, and the many encounters with the West. We will examine the politics, cultures, social norms, and different peoples, with a focus on the problem of modernization.

nodes.title: Modern China (Since 1911)
nodes.prereq_text: Any lower-division course in History or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: The fall of the dynastic system, the revolution against traditional values, the rise of the Nationalist Party, the challenge from the Communists, the founding of the People's Republic, and the Post-Mao reform, focusing on the theme of revolution.

nodes.title: Japan Under the Tokugawa Shoguns
nodes.prereq_text: History 2A or 2B or 2C or 9 or 87 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: A survey of Japanese social and cultural history from the mid-sixteenth century to the nineteenth century.

nodes.title: Modern Japan
nodes.prereq_text: History 2A or 2B or 2C or 9 or 87 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: A survey of Japanese history from the early nineteenth century until World War II, in an effort to explain how, and at what price, Japan became the first successful modernizer in the nonwestern world.

nodes.title: Recent Japan
nodes.prereq_text: History 2A or 2B or 2C or 9 or 87 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: The history of Japan since World War II, dealing with the American occupation, economic recovery and growth, social change, and political development.

nodes.title: The Samurai
nodes.prereq_text: Hist 9 or 80 or 87 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: The samurai of Japan were a hereditary military class that evolved over a millennium. Course traces this history and clarifies the range of differences that separated samurai in each era as their roles and ideologies changed.

nodes.title: History of Women in China: From the Ancient Period to the Nineteenth Century
nodes.description: Exploration of the diverse roles women have played in Chinese culture and society up to the 19th century by examining the many contexts within which women operated: the family, the imperial court, literati and popular culture.

nodes.title: South Asian Public Culture
nodes.description: Historical and contemporary forms of South Asian expressive and popular culture, including cinema, television, popular music, material culture, performance, and literature. Focuses on relations among popular culture, everyday life and social history in post-colonial South Asia.

nodes.title: First-Year Japanese I
nodes.description: An introduction to modern Japanese. Students will develop basic communicative skills based on the fundamentals of grammar, vocabulary, and conversational expressions. Emphasis on both oral-aural proficiency andwriting-reading skills. Introduction to Hiragana and Katakana syllabaries, and Kanji.

nodes.title: First-Year Japanese II
nodes.prereq_text: Japanese 1 with grade C or better, or equivalent.
nodes.description: Continuation of Japanese 1.

nodes.title: First-Year Japanese III
nodes.prereq_text: Japanese 2 with grade C or better, or equivalent
nodes.description: Continuation of Japanese 2.

nodes.title: Second-Year Japanese
nodes.prereq_text: Japanese 3 with grade C or better, or equivalent
nodes.description: Continuation of Japanese 3. Course emphasizes the further development of both oral-aural proficiency and reading-writing skills with an intensive review of basic grammar as well as an introduction to more advanced grammar, vocabulary, and Kanji.

nodes.title: Second-Year Japanese
nodes.prereq_text: Japanese 4 with grade C or better, or equivalent
nodes.description: Continuation of Japanese 4.

nodes.title: Second-Year Japanese
nodes.prereq_text: Japanese 5 with grade C or better, or equivalent
nodes.description: Continuation of Japanese 5.

nodes.title: Imagining the Samurai
nodes.description: A critical exploration of the image and myth of the samurai, Japan's hereditary warrior class, as constructed in Japanese literature, film, drama and art.

nodes.title: Violence and the Japanese State
nodes.description: Examines historiographically and sociologically the Japanese State's various engagements in violent acts during war and peace times.

nodes.title: Sociology of Japan
nodes.description: Sociological macro- and micro-analysis of Japanese society in the twentieth century.

nodes.title: Introduction to Japanese Religion: Texts, Concepts, and Representations
nodes.description: A survey of the main authors, themes, and styles of the Japanese religious and philosophical traditions through readings from and analysis of some significant and influential original texts in English translation.

nodes.title: Masterpieces of Japanese Literature
nodes.description: Examines a selection of works from Japanese literature, with the goal of understanding the major genres and their development over time. The cultural roles of literature, as well as criteria for critical evaluation, are also addressed.

nodes.title: Japanese Folklore
nodes.description: Introduction to Japanese folklore and folklore studies. Concepts, categories, and methodologies of folklore studies will be applied to the narrative, life cycle, and material forms of Japanese folklore. Course also examines motives and aims of Japanese folklorists over time.

nodes.title: Survey of Modern Japanese Literature
nodes.description: A survey of Japanese literature after contact with the West, from 1868 to the present. Readings, lectures, and discussions in English.

nodes.title: Topics in Twentieth-Century Japanese
nodes.description: Topics to be considered will include: the Japanese novelist as intellectual and social critic; representations of the self and similarities and differences between the shosetsu and the western novel; and Japanese literature in and outside Japan.

nodes.title: Third-Year Japanese I
nodes.prereq_text: Japanese 6 with grade C or better, or equivalent
nodes.description: Develops an intermediate to advanced level of aural-oral skills to carry on conversations on diverse topics with linguistic accuracy and cultural appropriateness, reading skills to comprehend authentic materials, and writing skills with grammatical accuracy and an increasing number of Kanji.

nodes.title: Third-Year Japanese II
nodes.prereq_text: Japanese 120A with grade C or better, or equivalent
nodes.description: Continuation of Japanese 120A.

nodes.title: Third-Year Japanese III
nodes.prereq_text: Japanese 120B with grade C or better, or equivalent.
nodes.description: Continuation of Japanese 120B.

nodes.title: Early Modern Japanese Literature
nodes.description: A survey (in English translation) of Japanese fiction, poetry, and drama from the early modern period, or approximately 1600 to 1868. Topics include popular fiction, supernatural tales, travel literature, haikai and haiku, and puppet theater and kabuki.

nodes.title: Japanese Humor
nodes.description: An examination of humor and the comic tradition in Japanese culture and literature from earliest times through the present. Topics include comic fiction and poetry, parody and satire, comic storytelling and jokes, standup and slapstick, and TV variety shows.

nodes.title: Japanese Diasporas
nodes.description: This course explores the diverse people of Japanese descent in North America, Latin America, and Asia in the modern and contemporary periods. Students investigate how movements shape identities by analyzing a multicultural array of sources including books, articles, and movies.

nodes.title: Critical Theory Through Anime and Manga
nodes.description: This course teaches critical theories by combining academic texts by scholars and popular culture products such as anime and manga. The topics include power, hegemony, agency, ritual, magic, hybridity, among others.

nodes.title: Curiosity and Spectacle in Early Modern Japan
nodes.description: Cultural and intellectual movements of early modern (Edo) Japan explored through the themes of curiosity and spectacle. Travel, material culture, print media, popular fiction and theater, sideshows and street performers, natural history, the supernatural, the study of foreign cultures and of the past.

nodes.title: Advanced Japanese Readings I
nodes.description: Designed to further develop skills in reading by focusing on analysis of Japanese sentence structure.

nodes.title: Advanced Japanese Readings II
nodes.description: Introduces advanced students to selected prose and poetry from post-World War II period.

nodes.title: Death, Love & Money in Modern Japan
nodes.description: How does capitalism remake intimacy and love? How does kinship shape the experiences of aging and death? What is relationship between gender and economy? Students explore these key questions by examining theoretical texts, movies, anime, and manga, among others.

nodes.title: The Cultural Roots of the Japanese Horror Film
nodes.description: From classical tales of noblemen and warriors to ghost dramas of medieval and early modern Japan, we will explore premodern creative expression concerning ghosts and their modern appearances in horror films and anime. Texts, images, and film will be used.

nodes.title: Japanese Cinema
nodes.description: An introductory scrutiny of major Japanese directors: Mizoguchi, Ozu, Oshima, and Kurosawa. Close attention to their film composition, choices ofsubject and character, their ideas of the cinematic, and the relationship of cinema to Japanese culture and society.

nodes.title: Ethnic and Social Diversity in Japan
nodes.description: Examines how difference is conceptualized and camouflaged in Japan despite an ideology of ethnic homogeneity. Considers the history and development of, and contemporary politics within internal and external minority communities and their diasporas across Japan.

nodes.title: Representations of Sexuality in Modern Japan
nodes.description: This course examines the main ideologies guiding the establishment of various representations of sexuality from prewar scientific writings to contemporary popular culture.

nodes.title: Modernity and the Masses of Taisho Japan
nodes.prereq_text: History 80 or 87 or Upper Division Standing
nodes.description: Examines the beginnings of a modern mass culture in early twentieth- century Japan. Central topics are political and social movements, the new woman and the modern girl, westernization, new media and censorship, modernism and nationalism.

nodes.title: Popular Culture in Japan
nodes.description: Examines popular culture in present-day Japan: advertising, music, fashion, television, animation, comics, sports. Integrates visual and acoustic material.

nodes.title: Body and Self in Japanese Culture
nodes.description: Addresses how historians, anthropologists, artists, creators of popular culture, film makers, and literary authors have attached meanings to the human body and its relation to selfhood since the 19th century.

nodes.title: Religion in Japanese Culture
nodes.description: A historical analysis of the major components of the classical and medieval religious systems of Japan, through investigation of texts, rituals, and institutions.

nodes.title: Seminar in Traditional Japanese Theater
nodes.description: Survey and in-depth examinations of specific selected topics in traditional Japanese theater. Knowledge of Japanese not required.

nodes.title: Shinto through the Ages
nodes.description: Explores the diversity of the Shinto tradition through an analysis of representative original texts in English translation ranging from ancient mythology (Kojiki, Nihon shoki, and Fudoki) and medieval syncretic discourses, to modern forms of Shinto nationalism.

nodes.title: Introduction to Classical Japanese
nodes.description: Introduction to classical Japanese grammar, vocabulary, and major genres. Foundation for the study of premodern through prewar texts. Prerequisite for JAPAN 183.

nodes.title: Readings in Premodern through Meiji Japanese Texts
nodes.description: Selected readings in medieval, early modern, and Meiji texts.

nodes.title: Readings in Japanese
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Japaneseconsent of instructor.

nodes.description: Guided reading in Japanese on a subject not covered in the regularly offered courses.

nodes.title: Independent Studies in Japanese
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Japanese; at least one of those two courses taken with instructor for Japan 199; GPA for those two courses 3.5 or higher

items.text: completion of 2 upper-division courses in Japanese

nodes.description: Individual investigations in literary fields.

nodes.title: First Year Korean
nodes.description: The beginning course in Korean. The student acquires a basic knowledge of the grammar, a limited general vocabulary, correct pronunciation, and an ability to read and understand simple texts. Weekly laboratory assignments support and enhance classroom learning.

nodes.title: First Year Korean
nodes.description: Continuation of Korean 1.

nodes.title: First Year Korean
nodes.description: Continuation of Korean 2.

nodes.title: Second Year Korean
nodes.description: Continuation of Korean 3.

nodes.title: Second Year Korean
nodes.description: Continuation of Korean 4.

nodes.title: Second Year Korean
nodes.description: Continuation of Korean 5.

nodes.title: Korean Literature Survey
nodes.description: Introduces Korea's award winning authors from the 17th century romance to contemporary period women's literature. Topics include class stratification in Yangban society, Japanese occupation, the Korean War, the politics of division, urbanization, prostitution, and alienation.

nodes.title: Advanced Korean
nodes.description: A course designed to develop ability in reading contemporary Korean essays,literary works, magazines, and newspapers. Emphasis on solidfying students' grammatical foundation, mastery of Hanja and vocabulary, and proficiency in writing and oral skills.

nodes.title: Korean War in Literature and Film
nodes.description: Examines the representations of the Korean War in transnational literature and film. All reading, viewing, and listening material will be available in English translation.

nodes.title: Cultures of Protest in South Korea
nodes.description: This course engages with diverse medialiterature, music, film, digital mediato explore how culture is mobilized as an active site of protest in South Korea. All reading, viewing, and listening material will be available in English translation.

nodes.title: Korean Popular Culture
nodes.description: This course engages with diverse media—literature, music, film, digital media—as active sites of cultural production, distribution, and consumption in modern and contemporary Korea. All reading, viewing, and listening material will be available in English translation.

nodes.title: Readings in Korean
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Korean. Consent of instructor.

items.text: completion of 2 upper-division courses in Korean

nodes.description: Guided reading in Korean on a subject not covered in the regularly offered courses.

nodes.title: EMS: Approaches to University Writing for Multilingual Students
nodes.prereq_text: Open to students who have not satisfied the Entry Level Writing Requirement and have a Ling 12 placement or a prerequisite of Ling 3C with a grade of C or better.

requires.text: Open to students who have not satisfied the Entry Level Writing Requirement and have a LING 12 placement or a prerequisite of LING 3C

nodes.description: Principles of critical reading, thinking and writing in the university. Students analyze academic discourse, develop rhetorical strategies for exposition and argument, practice examination writing, and write and revise papers. Completion of C or better meets Entry Level Writing Requirement.

nodes.title: Introduction to Asian Religious Traditions
nodes.description: An introduction to the basic texts, institutions, and practices of the religious traditions of South Asia and East Asia.

nodes.title: Introduction to Buddhism
nodes.description: The historical and cross-cultural exploration of Buddhism through the examination of basic texts, institutions, and practices of diverse Buddhist traditions.

nodes.title: Zen Buddhism
nodes.description: An introduction to the history and texts of the major lineages of Ch`an Buddhism in China and Zen Buddhism in Japan.

nodes.title: Contemporary Chinese Religions
nodes.description: Examines Chinese popular religion, Daoism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Christianity, and Islam as shaped and transformed by revolution and nationalism, and the recent rapid commercialization, urbanization, and globalization of China. Religiosity and changing notions of self, family, gender, community, and citizenship.

nodes.title: Introduction to Daoism
nodes.description: A study of the classical sources of Daoism, followed by a consideration of the varieties of religious practice which developed from those sources.

nodes.title: Introduction to Japanese Religion: Texts, Concepts, and Representations
nodes.description: A survey of the main authors, themes, and styles of the Japanese religious and philosophical traditions through readings from and analysis of some significant and influential original texts in English translation.

nodes.title: Christianity, Judaism, and Islam in China
nodes.description: Examines Christian, Jewish, and Muslim communities in the Middle Kingdom from 500 to the present day, debunking the myth of a closed and insular China.

nodes.title: Asian American Religions
nodes.prereq_text: Upper Division Standing or permission of instructor.
nodes.description: Historical and interdisciplinary approach to the themes and issues in the religious traditions of Asian Americans. Topics: the civil religious context, the transplantation of Asian traditions into the U.S., Asian American Christianity, Asian American theology.

nodes.title: Religious Environmentalism in the Anthropocene: Asia & U.S.
nodes.description: What can ancient religious traditions do for environmental protection? This class examines doctrinal examples, both potential and actual, of religious environmentalism in China, India, Japan, and the U.S. with Buddhism, Daoism, Hinduism, Shinto, and Protestantism.

nodes.title: Consciousness and the Body in Hindu Traditions
nodes.description: An exploration of Hindu constructions of embodiment and the relationship of the mind-body complex to consciousness. Critical analysis of discursive representations and practices in various Hindu traditions, including ritual traditions, ascetic movements, legal codes, medical discourses, devotional movements, and Tantric traditions.

nodes.title: Religion in Japanese Culture
nodes.description: A historical analysis of the major components of the classical and medieval religious systems of Japan, through investigation of texts, rituals, and institutions.

nodes.title: Shinto through the Ages
nodes.description: Explores the diversity of the Shinto tradition through an analysis of representative original texts in English translation ranging from ancient mythology (Kojiki, Nihon shoki, and Fudoki) and medieval syncretic discourses, to modern forms of Shinto nationalism.

nodes.title: Visual Culture of Buddhism
nodes.description: This course explores the rich world of Buddhist visual culture, ranging from meditation to addressing the use of painted images in public performances. It focuses on sacred images, their rituals, and theories of representation behind their creation and use.

nodes.title: Religious Practice and the State in China
nodes.description: Historical and anthropological approaches to the interaction between religious practice and state forces, with emphasis on popular religion and the decline and revival of religion in Chinese modernity.

nodes.title: Religion and Healing in Global Perspective
nodes.description: Comparative and cross-cultural introduction to relationships between religion, science, and healing arts, using selected case studies and stressing alternatives to mainstream western medicine. Attention to underlying religio-philosophical worldviews and to the ways in which they influence healing practices.

nodes.title: Performance in Global Contexts: ASIA
nodes.description: This course surveys a range of Asian performances across a diversity of locations, from the traditional theater forms of Japanese Kabuki, Indonesian Wayang Kulit, and Indian Kathakali to modern forms in India and Japan to contemporary Chinese performance art. Theater forms like Chinese Jingju and Japanese Noh will prompt us to reevaluate what the performer does in rehearsal and in situations on and off the stage. By exploring recent modern and contemporary performance forms, we will reassess how an actor, dancer, or puppeteer can challenge the status quo and effect change. As we ask these questions, we will situate Asian performance within social, political, and historical contexts to understand its rich functions and significances.

nodes.title: Academic Writing
nodes.prereq_text: Satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing requirement or Linguistics 12 with a grade of "C" or better.

items.text: Satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing requirement

nodes.description: A writing course focusing on developing analytical skills, synthesizing multiple sources, sustaining coherent arguments, and revising for clarity of style. Reading and writing assignments are drawn from a range of academic disciplines.
